title: Stability of Euler's Method
short: For y′ = λy with λ < 0, Euler's method gives yₙ = (1 + hλ)ⁿ y₀, which stays bounded only when |1 + hλ| ≤ 1, that is, when h ≤ 2/|λ|.
trouble: Students think a method with small truncation error works with any step size. When h is too large for the problem, the steps blow up even though the true solution decays.

blocks.html: A method with small truncation error can still produce garbage if the step is too big, even when the true solution is perfectly calm. To see why, apply it to the test equation $$y' = \lambda y,\qquad \text{Re}\,\lambda < 0,$$ whose solution $y_0e^{\lambda t}$ decays. This is the ODE version of algorithm stability.

Euler's method gives $y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + h\lambda)y_n$, so $$y_n = (1 + h\lambda)^{n}y_0.$$ Every one-step method turns into $y_{n+1} = R(h\lambda)\,y_n$ for some function $R$, its amplification factor.

The computed values stay bounded only when $|R(h\lambda)| \le 1$. For forward Euler, $R(z) = 1 + z$, so $h\lambda$ must lie in the disk of radius 1 centered at $-1$; for real $\lambda < 0$ that means $h \le \frac{2}{|\lambda|}$. For a system $\mathbf{y}' = A\mathbf{y}$, every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ must satisfy the condition.

The exact solution decays because $|e^{h\lambda}| < 1$. The method replaces $e^{h\lambda}$ by $R(h\lambda)$, which is accurate for small $|h\lambda|$ (it matches the Taylor series of $e^{z}$ up to the method's order) but can be larger than 1 in size when $|h\lambda|$ is large. Then $|R|^{n}$ grows without bound, and any error, even round-off, is magnified each step. For a system, diagonalizing $A$ splits it into separate test equations, one per eigenvalue, so the step must suit the eigenvalue farthest from the origin.

blocks.title: Too big a step
steps: $h = 0.15$: $R = -0.5$: the values decay, with a wrong-signed wiggle.
$h = 0.05$: $R = 0.5$: smooth decay, as $e^{-10t}$ does. The limit is $h = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2$.

blocks.title: A stiff system
blocks.q: A linear system has eigenvalues $-1$ and $-1000$. What step does forward Euler need?
steps: So $h \le 0.002$, a thousand times smaller than accuracy for the slow part would require, even after the fast part has died away. Such a system is stiff.

blocks.title: A complex eigenvalue
blocks.q: For $\lambda = -1 + 3i$ (a decaying oscillation), find the largest stable $h$ for forward Euler.
steps: So $h \le \frac{2}{10} = 0.2$. In general $h \le \frac{2|\text{Re}\,\lambda|}{|\lambda|^{2}}$; for nearly undamped oscillations this gets tiny.

blocks.html: Thinking a method with small truncation error works with any step size. Accuracy is about small $h$; stability is about $|R(h\lambda)| \le 1$. Past the stability limit the steps blow up even though the true solution decays, and a higher-order explicit method does not fix it (RK4's limit is only a little larger). Check: estimate the most negative eigenvalue and keep $h|\lambda|$ inside the method's region, or switch to an implicit method.
